article.title: How American History Celebrates Enslavers and Erases Their Victims
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Recently, a friend asked whether I had seen the documentary Natchez . Knowing of my involvement in Coming to the Table , he sent a link, encouraged me to watch, and asked whether I would write about it afterward. Coming to the Table brings together descendants of enslaved people and enslavers, along with others committed to racial justice, to uncover history, build relationships, pursue healing, and take action. Through that work, I have come to know Tom DeWolf, a founding member and longtime leader. His ancestors, the DeWolfs of Bristol, Rhode Island, were the largest slave-trading family in U.S. history, responsible for trafficking approximately 10,000 Africans into slavery. Tom joined nine relatives on a journey confronting that history, documented in Traces of the Trade: A Story from the Deep North and his book, Inheriting the Trade . His work asks whose suffering supplied a family’s wealth and what responsibilities follow from knowing that truth. Those questions shaped my viewing of Natchez . Watching it left me gutted. As a Black woman descended from enslaved people, I cannot separate this history from my ancestors’ lives. The persistent disregard for their pain hurts. Watching that disregard persist among people alive today adds another injury. Natchez exposes competing accounts of the plantation South. Black guides and preservationists challenge the mythology. The film’s willingness to expose it matters. What gutted me was the continuing appetite for the fantasy it documents. In 2026, there is still a market for plantation grandeur that keeps the people whose captivity sustained it at an emotional distance. Houses become treasures. Enslavers maintain the veneer of accomplished gentlemen. The people they brutalized are little more than background. A documentary needs an audience to be made and distributed. Audiences can seek confrontation with history or reassurance about it. Natchez brings those competing desires into view. My indictment is of the continuing acceptance and appetite for the antebellum myth: the desire to enjoy the beauty without fully facing its brutality and the human cost. I have encountered that desire intimately. Years ago, I dated a man who told me slavery was wrong but insisted we could not judge the Founders by today’s standards. I ended the relationship that day. His defense asked me to accommodate his admiration for the founders while accepting his emotional distance from hundreds of people they harmed and the generations descended from them. I could not build intimacy with someone whose admiration mattered more to him than my ancestors humanity. Enslaved people did not need today’s standards to understand the wrong being done to them. Their resistance, escapes, and testimony bore witness to their suffering at the hands of tormentors we continue to deify—and to their rejection of a system whose brutality admirers of enslavers still find ways to excuse. My ancestors’ suffering was historical. His unwillingness to take it seriously was happening then, to me, the Black woman standing before him. Consider how differently we recognize captivity elsewhere. In 1991, Phillip Garrido and his wife, Nancy, abducted eleven-year-old Jaycee Dugard. They held her captive for eighteen years. Beginning when Jaycee was 11 years old, Phillip repeatedly raped her; she gave birth at fourteen and seventeen. In Austria, Josef Fritzl imprisoned his eighteen-year-old daughter, Elisabeth, in a cellar for twenty-four years, repeatedly raping her. She bore seven children; one died in infancy. Both men were convicted and imprisoned. Garrido received 431 years to life; Fritzl received life imprisonment. Their crimes were recognized as horrific violations of human beings. Before their arrests, Garrido and Fritzl had careers. Garrido operated his own printing business. Fritzl was an electrical engineer and rental-property owner. Now imagine documentaries inviting us to admire Garrido’s entrepreneurship or Fritzl’s engineering accomplishments. Imagine mentioning their victims briefly before returning to the men’s achievements. Who would buy a ticket to see that? - The producers would be hard pressed to find a market that could stomach that distortion of the facts. Yet change the setting to a plantation, and the arrangement becomes familiar. The brutality required to hold hundreds of people captive recedes from the story. Admirers come for the gowns, the table settings, the grandeur. Imagine presenting Hitler’s home that way: inviting visitors to admire his taste while relegating his victims to the background. We would recognize the obscenity. Why does plantation nostalgia still find a willing audience in the United States? Harriet Jacobs, who escaped slavery and became an abolitionist, described her enslaver’s relentless sexual pursuit in her 1861 autobiography, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl . She testified to the terror of girlhood under another person’s claimed ownership. Under hereditary slavery, children inherited their mother’s enslaved status. An enslaver could rape a woman and claim the resulting child—even his own child—as property to work, inherit, or sell. The resemblance to modern captivity is therefore substantive: control over bodies, labor, movement, and children. Legal cover enlarged the perpetrator’s power and wealth. It did nothing to diminish the victim’s suffering. Black men lived under that power, too. In his 1845 autobiography, Frederick Douglass described the violence and relentless labor imposed by Edward Covey: “I was broken in body, soul, and spirit.” Bloodied after a beating, he appealed to Thomas Auld, the man who claimed ownership of him. Auld sent him back, insisting Covey “was a good man.” That judgment echoes through our commemorations. How much cruelty can a celebrated man’s reputation absorb before admiration becomes indefensible? At Choctaw Hall, one of the mansions toured in the film, guide and co-owner David Garner recounts defending Southern gentlemen against an accusation of arrogance: “We’re just proud of what we accomplished.” He credits seven generations of hard work for the surroundings visitors see. Whose work? Who built, cooked, cleaned, cultivated, and served? Whose captivity generated wealth? Where are their names when family pride takes center stage? The market for this selective memory was cultivated. After the Civil War, the Lost Cause movement promoted honorable Confederates, benevolent enslavers, and faithful enslaved people. Monuments, entertainment, and commemorations carried those images into national life. Confederate defeat opened the possibility for another future. During Reconstruction, Black Americans voted, held office, and built institutions. But white supremacists successfully fought those gains through terror and political resistance. As a result, federal protection receded. The former Confederate insurrectionists regained power, established Jim Crow and the racialized terror of lynching. That outcome was made possible by political choices in both the North and the South. Popular culture helped sustain it by romanticizing the defeated Confederacy while marginalizing the people it fought to keep enslaved. The blockbuster success of Gone with the Wind reveals how eagerly audiences embraced that mythology. Germany’s reckoning with Nazism was neither immediate nor complete. Nevertheless, its eventual official culture of remembrance made acknowledgment of Nazi crimes a national responsibility. Not so in the United States which has continued to uphold admiration for enslavers by distancing them from the implications of historical truth. That protection has contemporary consequences. When exploitation disappears from the history of wealth, inherited advantage looks entirely earned. When imposed disadvantage disappears, racial inequality looks like Black failure. Demands for repair then look like requests for undeserved favors. The injury also reaches beyond money. We learn whose pain requires an explanation before it deserves concern. I believe that habit connects the minimization of enslaved people’s suffering to the excuses made for mistreating Black people today, including by law enforcement. Authority receives the benefit of the doubt. The injured person must establish innocence, compliance, or respectability before receiving empathy. What did he do? Why didn’t he comply? Was the officer afraid? These questions can shift attention away from whether the person exercising power acted justly. Historical defenses can perform a similar function: explaining the powerful while distancing us from those they harmed. No single cause explains unequal policing. But the danger is documented. A 2019 study found that Black men and women faced greater lifetime risks of being killed by police than their white counterparts. Research also shows that Black pain can be discounted. A 2016 study found that white medical students and residents who endorsed false beliefs about biological racial differences made less accurate assessments of Black patients’ pain and less accurate treatment recommendations. That study concerns medicine. It nevertheless demonstrates that assumptions about Black bodies can affect whether suffering receives an adequate response. The stories we circulate can challenge those assumptions or leave them comfortable and undisturbed. This is a public safety issue. Black people are part of the public. Our safety cannot be expendable in the pursuit of someone else’s sense of order. After George Floyd’s murder, Coming to the Table explicitly connected police violence with the responsibility to transform institutions sustaining white supremacy. That connection explains why I belong at the table. Truth-telling must lead to changes in conduct, policy, and accountability. Healing cannot mean asking injured people to make peace with everyone else’s comfort. When someone says slavery happened too long ago to matter, I wonder why that reasoning applies to the debt but never to the inheritance. The mansions of Natchez embody wealth created through uncompensated labor. Why is it too late to compensate the descendants of the people whose labor created that wealth, but never too late for others to inherit its benefits? And why, in 2026, does an audience still want a version of that history organized around the enslaver’s pride? That appetite is the indictment. Every generation decides what it will celebrate and whose suffering it will accommodate. Today’s indifference is another injury, inflicted by people who can choose differently. The friend who sent me Natchez asked what I thought. I’m left asking: Whose history are we preserving when the enslaver’s reputation receives more protection than his victims ever did—and whose safety are we compromising when we carry that same hierarchy of concern into the present? These references cover the article’s main factual claims and offer readers further context. Natchez — PBS Independent Lens Official film page. The PBS transcript includes David Garner’s statements about accomplishment and seven generations of work. Independent Lens Coming to the Table — About Us Explains the organization’s origins and its practices of uncovering history, building relationships, pursuing healing, and taking action. Coming To The Table Traces of the Trade: A Story from the Deep North — Tracing Center Documents the DeWolf family’s involvement in trafficking more than 10,000 Africans and the descendants’ journey confronting that history. Tracing Center Inheriting the Trade — Thomas Norman DeWolf DeWolf’s account of the family journey and his confrontation with the legacy of slavery. tomdewolf.com Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl — Harriet Jacobs, 1861 Full text of Jacobs’s firsthand account. Chapter V, “The Trials of Girlhood,” is particularly relevant to the article’s discussion of sexual predation. Project Gutenberg Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave — 1845 Chapter X contains Douglass’s account of Edward Covey, his appeal to Thomas Auld, and his resistance. It supplies the quotations used in the article. www.gutenberg.org Virginia’s 1662 Law Making Children’s Status Follow Their Mother’s — Encyclopedia Virginia Reproduces the colonial statute establishing hereditary enslavement through the mother. encyclopediavirginia.org “The Civil War in American Memory” — David W. Blight, National Park Service Explains the Lost Cause, white sectional reconciliation, and the marginalization of emancipation in public memory. Also discusses Gone with the Wind as part of that cultural legacy. nps.gov Reconstruction Era — National Park Service Background on Black citizenship, political participation, and the reversal of Reconstruction’s gains through disenfranchisement and Jim Crow. Reconstruction Era (U.S. National Park Service) Memorial Sites — German Federal Government Describes Germany’s official responsibility for remembering Nazi crimes and commemorating their victims. bundesregierung.de Jaycee Dugard: Sentencing Statements and Grand-Jury Testimony — KQED Reporting and linked testimony concerning Dugard’s captivity and the Garridos’ sentences. KQED “Fritzl Gets Life Sentence for Murder, Rape, Imprisonment” — ABC News, 2009 Documents Josef Fritzl’s convictions, including rape and enslavement, and his life sentence. ABC News “Risk of Being Killed by Police Use of Force in the United States by Age, Race–Ethnicity, and Sex” — Edwards, Lee, and Esposito, 2019 Peer-reviewed research supporting the article’s statement about racial disparities in the lifetime risk of being killed by police. PubMed “Racial Bias in Pain Assessment and Treatment Recommendations, and False Beliefs About Biological Differences Between Blacks and Whites” — Hoffman and colleagues, 2016 The study linking false racial beliefs among white medical students and residents with biased pain assessments and treatment recommendations. pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov Coming to the Table Statement on Police Violence — July 2020 Explicitly connects George Floyd’s murder, racial justice, reparations, and institutional transformation. comingtothetable.org
